review: ⭐️💡📄 Запрос функции: встроенный рендеринг .md файлов в Telegram
rating:
**Проблема**
Telegram воспринимает .md файлы как обычные вложения. Чтобы прочитать README, техническую документацию или заметку, присланную в чат, нужно скачать файл и открыть его в отдельном приложении. Это прерывает рабочий процесс — особенно неудобно на мобильном.

**Что прошу добавить**
Нативный предпросмотр .md файлов с рендерингом Markdown — открывается прямо в Telegram при нажатии на файл, без выхода из приложения.

Предпросмотр должен поддерживать стандартные элементы Markdown:
• Заголовки (# H1, ## H2 и т.д.)
• **Жирный**, *курсив*, ~~зачёркнутый~~
• `Инлайн-код` и блоки кода с подсветкой синтаксиса
• Нумерованные и маркированные списки
• Цитаты
• Гиперссылки
• Горизонтальные разделители

**Предлагаемый UX:**
1. .md файл в чате — отображается с иконкой документа и меткой «Markdown»
2. Нажатие → полноэкранный рендеред-просмотр внутри Telegram
3. Иконка переключения (≡) между отрендеренным и исходным видом
4. Стандартные действия (поделиться, скопировать, скачать) остаются доступны

**Почему именно в Telegram**
Telegram уже парсит и рендерит Markdown в тексте сообщений и Bot API. Движок существует — применить его к предпросмотру .md файлов — это точечное, хорошо ограниченное улучшение, а не новая технология с нуля.

Разработчики, open-source команды, технические писатели и специалисты по документации постоянно делятся .md файлами. Нативная поддержка убрала бы лишнее трение и оставила весь рабочий процесс внутри приложения.

Спасибо, что рассматриваете этот запрос.

rating:
This app needs a confirmation warning before exiting or losing a temporary chat.

I just lost hours of work on a disability appeal because the chat was labeled “temporary,” but there was no clear, unavoidable warning that it would be permanently deleted. The label is small, black text at the top, and with low eyesight I did not see it. I normally do not need assistive readers to use ChatGPT, but apparently I did in this case just to catch that critical detail.

There was also no confirmation dialog when leaving the chat.

A small label in low-visibility formatting is not an adequate safeguard for something this important. This should be treated like unsaved work in any other application.

At minimum, you need:
• A clear, high-visibility warning that the chat will not be saved  
• A confirmation dialog before exiting or closing the chat  
• An option to convert a temporary chat into a saved one  

Losing important work without a safeguard is unacceptable, especially when users are working on critical documents.

Hours of work chewed up and spit out into slush. :/ I promptly closed the app and stopped writing in it.

You prompted me for a review on the right day. I’ve a long-time user of Notion - first tried it back in 2018 maybe? Don’t quote me on that, time is nebulous. It’s been a long time - that’s all I mean. For me to use any app/tool for this long speaks volumes about how useful it is.

I’ve tried every productivity/note-taking app on the market. I swear. Todoist, Trello, Tiimo, Chaos Control, Maple, Asana, Habitica, etc. I’ve tried GTD, mind maps, recording voice memos, habit trackers, to-do lists, and handwritten journals. I won’t lie, I get distracted by every shiny new productivity app I stumble across. But Notion is the only one that works for me, and it works well. So I always end up coming back to Notion.

The ability to build a database that links all of my ideas in one hub has allowed me to ACTUALLY take action on that big creative project I always said I wanted to do. I honestly thought my desire wasn’t strong enough because I always failed to follow through, but it turns out I was just lacking the right tools to help me get the job done. I’ve consistently published my newsletter for 21 weeks, two  times a week. If you have ADHD or know someone with it, you know how big of an accomplishment this is. Notion has the only tool I use outside of Beehiiv. 

My neurodivergent brain needed something built by me, for me. Not a prebuilt template created by someone who thinks differently than I do. (Although Notion has a TON of templates to help get you started!) I didn’t use Notion to its fullest potential for the first few years because I was limiting myself to those templates. I was afraid to try to build a database without having the finished picture in mind. I eventually got frustrated enough and started building my own. At first it was messy and chaotic, but now it is a system that reflects my thought processes and fits my needs perfectly.

I loved Notion enough as it was, but the addition of Notion AI has solidified this as my go-to tool for the rest of forever. Notion AI can now find my notes for me. I no longer have to search through months of random (and terribly named) Google Docs or search through a bookshelf of journals/planners to find past notes. And it helps me generate new ideas from my existing data with way less effort. 

I use Notion solo, but I’m sure it would be just as useful for a team. Highly recommend you give this app a try. And don’t just toy around with someone else’s template. Spend time building a system built for your unique needs & behaviors!

I've been a diehard Evernote user for about a year, but I decided to make the leap to Notion after seeing it numerous times on social media. I'm amazed at all the customization options—but consistently underwhelmed by the app's actual functionality. A lot of the features that are relatively easy on desktop just don't exist or don't work at all on the mobile version, making it impossible to edit my pages and templates on-the-go. How is it that you can't search the page for keywords? Why is it that I can't italicize words if it's inside a gallery page? 

I'm frankly annoyed and starting to regret trying to transfer all of my writing materials over from Evernote upon realizing that I can't probably copy and paste text—the first line appears, and the rest just teleports somewhere else on the page. Evernote is pretty bare bones when it comes to features, but at least their functionality is top notch. Notion is an aesthetic mess that I want to love so badly, but even putting aside the insane learning curve needed to use it, the UI and functionality is just genuinely bad.

rating:
If you like wasting 25 min in the morning while waiting through 4 cancellations from drivers who are en route in SG, this is the ride share app for you. 

Some interesting observations: 

• I typically book grab for my morning commute. But sometimes my partner books, and we’ve noticed consistent price disparities anywhere from 50 cents to as much as $5 when we are both searching simultaneously. Why is that? Is it because the algorithm? 🤷🏽‍♂️

• I saw a driver using a fare compare app on a recent ride…surely undercutting the value to riders using Grab or other ride shares. Can’t blame them. I’d do the same as a driver. 

• And just yesterday, a driver cancelled after nearly 10 minutes, despite being just around the corner at his prior drop off, and to book a new driver, price increased from $11.30 to $23.90. So let’s all start calling dynamic pricing what it really is: dynamic price gouging. 

Great in other SE Asia countries as you avoid scam pricing. And overall, convenience created by door front pick up is excellent for these apps, but it’s starting to feel like “actually, maybe regular taxis ARE better.”

rating:
Uber holds over 75% of the U.S. rideshare market and pays its drivers the equivalent of about $9.21/hr after expenses, commissions, and the cost of benefits they don’t receive — placing them near the bottom 10% of wage earners nationally.

Uber calls its drivers “independent contractors,” which means no minimum wage, no overtime, no workers’ comp, no unemployment, and no right to unionize. But drivers can’t set their own prices, can’t build their own customer relationships, and can be deactivated by an algorithm without meaningful recourse. An analysis under the Department of Labor’s own economic reality test finds they function far more like employees than contractors.

Uber spent massively to pass Prop 22 in California — preserving their labor model by ballot initiative after courts began ruling against them. They’ve repeated the playbook in other states. When the law starts to catch up, they buy more time.

For Uber Eats specifically: NYC found their interface design tricks, implemented in 2023, deliberately suppressed tips — driving average tip per delivery down to $0.76, compared to $2.17 on competing platforms. $554 million in combined tip losses with DoorDash. At that point, is it really a “choice,” or just a way to squeeze more money out of users?

I’d seriously recommend trying other ride apps. They might have their own issues, but at least you’re not feeding into what feels like a monopoly taking advantage of its customers.

review: Grateful for the service, but the pay breakdown feels off

That said, after looking more closely at my most recent ride, I noticed the driver received about 47% of what I paid. I understand there are fees and operational costs involved, but it was surprising and honestly a bit disheartening to see how the breakdown actually works.

I’m sharing this not as a complaint, but as feedback — I’d love to see more transparency or a more balanced distribution that better supports drivers, who are the core of the experience.

Overall, I’m grateful for the service and will continue using it, but I hope this is something that continues to improve over time.

review: Remove the repost button right now immediately!!
rating:
The repost button on Instagram is one of the most poorly thought-out UX decisions they’ve made in years—and that’s saying something.

It sits in a position where your thumb naturally rests while scrolling, meaning accidental taps aren’t just possible—they’re inevitable. This isn’t a rare “oops” moment; it’s a repeatable, built-in failure of the interface. Any competent product design team should know that high-impact actions (like publicly reposting content to your followers) require friction, confirmation, or at minimum intentional placement. Instead, Instagram did the opposite: they made it frictionless and dangerously easy to trigger.

The result? Users are unknowingly broadcasting content they never intended to share. That’s not just annoying—it’s reputationally risky. One accidental repost can misrepresent your taste, opinions, or even professional image. There’s no buffer, no meaningful safeguard—just instant, irreversible exposure unless you catch it immediately.

From a design principles standpoint, it violates basic UX fundamentals:
	•	No confirmation step for a socially visible action
	•	Poor button placement in a high-touch zone
	•	No undo grace period that’s clearly surfaced
	•	Ambiguous affordance—it doesn’t feel “dangerous” enough for what it does

It’s the equivalent of putting a “send to all contacts” button right next to your keyboard and hoping people don’t fat-finger it.

And the worst part: nobody was asking for this feature in the first place. Instagram already had sharing via stories and DMs—controlled, intentional channels. This repost button adds nothing but risk and noise to the platform while degrading user trust.

Bottom line: it should either be removed entirely or redesigned with:
	•	A confirmation prompt
	•	A less intrusive placement
	•	A clear visual distinction from passive actions

Right now, it’s not just a bad feature—it’s a liability disguised as convenience.

Instagram, a titan of social media, should be leading the charge in user experience and digital safety. Yet, this omission leaves users vulnerable and frustrated. It’s bewildering that a platform of Instagram’s caliber, with its vast resources and technical prowess, has not addressed this issue. The ability to hide comments during live streams is not just a matter of convenience; it’s a critical tool for safeguarding against harassment, spam, and the myriad of distractions that detract from the core experience.

Moreover, this limitation stifles creativity and expression. Content creators and influencers, who are the lifeblood of Instagram, rely on live features to connect authentically with their audience. The inability to curate this experience by hiding inappropriate or irrelevant comments can tarnish the quality of broadcasts and dissuade creators from utilizing this feature to its full potential.

In conclusion, Instagram’s failure to implement a basic yet crucial feature like hiding comments on live broadcasts is not just an oversight; it’s a significant flaw in the platform’s design. It reflects poorly on Instagram’s commitment to user experience and digital well-being. I urge Instagram to rectify this issue promptly. Until then, my disappointment compels me to rate the platform a disheartening one star.

rating:
This app gets a lot of attention as it tracks your progress, shows and gives you medals for your PR, and allows you to connect and share and get likes for accomplishments with other cyclist and runners.  I was suckered into paying for the full subscription by the hype this app gets with all the “if it isn’t logged on Strava it didn’t happen” acclaims.  Tonight I went on a near 4 hour ride and the app only tracked the duration and nothing else.  This app is overrated and glitchy to be useful.  

Map my ride is a much better app and you don’t need to pay extra to still get a great app experience.  Map my ride allows you to connect with other too but not as well as Strava.  However where it shines is if you want it to it gives you verbal updates in either variable time or distance increments with your current speed, distance, split pace, and average space.  Also what is cool is it will provide a starting timer so you don’t have to start the workout when you are stationary or just warming up.  

I actually did a quality test having both log a ride simultaneously and the stats were nearly the same however Strava gave me faster average speed so if you want to inflate your speed stats then Strava is for you.  

I now have to begrudgingly keep this app and make the best of it until my yearly subscription expires next January.  Don’t be a fool like me and give this app any of your money.   Keep it to humor your friends if you must.  Map my ride is so much better.

rating:
I downloaded Strava to “go on more walks.” What I got instead was a deeply intimate performance art platform that eroticizes productivity, surveillance, and self documentation in a way no dating app ever could.

There is nothing sexier than a glowing orange map of where I’ve been. Look at me. Witness me. I walked 4 miles and felt something. The pace? Slow. The elevation gain? Emotional. The time of day? Questionable. The commentary? Vulnerable enough to be inappropriate, but framed as “wellness.”

Strava knows when I’m active. It knows when I’m resting. It knows when I’m spiraling but calls it “recovery.” It rewards me with digital badges for consistency, which is frankly a kink. Every post feels like whispering into a public diary while pretending it’s just cardio.

Other apps ask, “What are you looking for Strava asks, “How did it feel?” And I answer. Every time.

For the most part, this is functional. I recently started using this instead of Nike Run Club in order to connect more with friends and family who exercise, and to be motivated by that. It is good for this. However, there are two large problems when compared to NRC.

(1) Free is stingy. With NRC you can always look up your best times (1 mile, 5K, 10K, etc.).   With Strava, for ***$80 per year*** you can see your best times. I mean, come on. I’m not asking for extremely detailed analysis of my exercise. This alone may have me going back to NRC at some point, or to record runs there after the fact.

(2) Glitchy auto-pause. In only 1 month using Strava, the auto-pause has randomly triggered twice for me and it remained on throughout the exercise until I saw it. This has happened with two family members and a friend in the past month, all who use different recording devices. Okay, so, I have removed autopause, but now need to remember to turn it off and on when I hit traffic signals.

Not the quality worth paying $80 for each year. Would I pay $10 one time to see my best times? Sure, I guess. But that’s not on the table.

rating:
Google Maps is decent overall, but the transit feature in Belgrade, Serbia often feels incomplete and unreliable.

It usually gives only one bus or tram option instead of showing useful alternatives. Many times, there are other workable routes, like taking one bus a few stops and then transferring, but the app does not suggest them. That makes trip planning more limiting than it should be.

The live transit timing is also inconsistent. Sometimes it says a bus or tram is on the way, but it does not clearly show when another one is arriving right after it, which would help with better choices.

The walking directions during transit also need improvement. When a transfer requires going to a stop on the other side of the street, the app does not always make that clear. In places with stops on both sides, it can be easy to board the right number going in the wrong direction. The directions should clearly say when to cross the street and which side or direction the tram or bus is heading.

It works well enough for basic navigation, but the transit guidance in Belgrade needs to be much more detailed and accurate.
